findings.claim: The scripture reference is written five times as "Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (391)" or "Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 391" (content_html twice, conclusion_html, exam_tip_html, practice_questions[4].marks).
findings.truth: "391" is not a citation. Upanishad references are chapter.section.verse, so the reference is Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.9.1. The spec markdown prints it with the full stops stripped. A student copying "391" into an exam cites nothing.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.4.1 bullet "Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 391"; Wikipedia, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, section 3.9.1

findings.claim: "2. Within the heart. The divine is also present within every living being as the inner self. This inner spark is called the atman." The takeaway and key fact repeat "within the heart - atman, the inner self".
findings.truth: The second feature is the divine dwelling in the heart, the inner controller (antaryami). That is not the same as the individual atman: in Vaishnava and Dvaita thought the indwelling divine accompanies the atman but stays distinct from it. Only Advaita identifies the two. The lesson names the term for feature 1 (brahman) and feature 3 (personal God) but leaves feature 2 unnamed and collapses it into atman.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.4.1, three features of the divine: "everywhere, as non-personal (brahman) / within the heart / beyond, as a personal loving God"; Wikipedia, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the inner controller (antaryamin) passage

findings.claim: "Confusing these terms is one of the most common errors examiners see."
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiners. No published source supports it. House rule: never assert what examiners see or reward.
findings.evidence: checker brief, fabricated examiner claims are FIX

findings.claim: practice_questions[2] is labelled "2 marks - State / Give" with a mark scheme reading "Maximum 2 marks".
findings.truth: This paper sets two five-part questions per religion of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks. No 2-mark question exists. Re-set as a 4-mark Explain, which the paper does use and which the lesson content supports.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1: "marks will be allocated as follows: 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12"; spec 2.2, 96 marks plus 6 SPaG, 1 hour 45 minutes

findings.claim: practice_questions[1] is labelled "2 marks - State / Give": "Name the four aims of human life (purusharthas) in Hinduism." with "Full 2 marks for all four named correctly".
findings.truth: Same as F4: no 2-mark question is set. Re-set as the 1-mark Name question, so the lesson matches the 1, 1, 4, 4, 6, 12 pattern used by lessons 2 and 3.

findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner behaviour. The teaching point itself is correct and is kept; the appeal to examiners is removed.

findings.claim: "ISKCON (the International Society for Krishna Consciousness), based at Bhaktivedanta Manor near Watford..."
findings.truth: ISKCON is a worldwide movement founded in New York in 1966, with its international headquarters at Mayapur in West Bengal. Bhaktivedanta Manor, at Aldenham near Watford, is its best-known British temple, not its base.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, International Society for Krishna Consciousness; Wikipedia, Bhaktivedanta Manor

findings.claim: "The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (391) sets out these three features clearly."
findings.truth: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.9.1 is the Yajnavalkya and Sakalya dialogue on how many gods there are: 3,306 reduced step by step to 33, 6, 3, 2, one and a half, and finally one. It does not itself set out the three features. The everywhere / within the heart / beyond scheme matches the brahman, paramatma, bhagavan triad usually traced to Bhagavata Purana 1.2.11. The board still names 3.9.1 in this bullet, so the citation is what the exam expects. Options: (a) keep the board's citation and drop only the word "clearly" and the claim that the verse sets the features out, which is what the edit does; (b) also add one clause saying 3.9.1 reduces the many gods to one Brahman; (c) leave the linkage unexplained.
findings.ruling: Leave: board citation kept; the overclaim is already removed by the edit.

findings.claim: Named individuals are quoted as real witnesses: "In Leicester, Priya, a 67-year-old grandmother..." (L1) and "In Birmingham, Deepa, a 45-year-old Shaivite Hindu..." (L3). L4 states that "At the Hindu Council UK's annual gatherings, community leaders often describe their tradition using the language of sanatana dharma".
findings.truth: These people and the quoted words are invented, and the Hindu Council UK claim is not sourced. Nothing here is examinable, so no marks are at risk, but the unit presents invented testimony as fieldwork and attributes a practice to a real named organisation.
findings.evidence: no source exists for the quotations or the Hindu Council UK claim

summary: Ten findings across four lessons: two practice questions carried an impossible 2-mark label (the paper sets 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12), three passages made up examiner or mark-scheme claims, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad reference was printed as '391' in five places, and the second feature of the divine was collapsed into atman with no mention of the indwelling divine (antaryami). Doctrine, deities, consorts, avatars, Sanskrit terms, the tri-guna, the four varnas and the four ashramas, the Rig Veda 10.129.6-7 cosmology reference and all twenty knowledge-check answer keys were correct.
